Unattended, always on, hard to reach: the hardest kind of edge device

0:45

  • You see signage every day: menu boards, departure screens, hospital wayfinding, factory dashboards
  • Behind each screen: a small computer, often a Pi, pulling content from a cloud dashboard
  • The catch: on 24/7, nobody watching, often bolted into a ceiling
  • One of the hardest edge workloads, which is why we needed Ubuntu Core
10,000+

Screenly players run Ubuntu Core today.
On board since 2016, one of the earliest adopters.

1:30

  • About 10,000 Screenly players run Ubuntu Core today: boardrooms, hospitals, shops, bus stops
  • We bet the product on it in May 2016, before Core 16 even shipped
  • No SSH, no engineers sent out when an update goes wrong
  • They update themselves and roll back on their own
  • That's the gap: a Pi that works on your desk vs one you can ship ten thousand times

From pets to cattle

🐶 Pets

Hand-tended, one of a kind. When sick, you nurse them back to health.

Your Pi on the desk.

🐄 Cattle

Identical, replaceable, known state. When sick, you replace them.

A fleet in the field.

Screenly, 2013: Puppet on ~10,000 Pis  ·  10-minute runs: pull the plug, brick a screen
Lesson: build the OS for cattle

1:30

  • Pets vs cattle comes from the cloud world; our Pi projects all start as pets
  • Screenly, 2013: about 10,000 players managed with Puppet
  • Each run took around 10 minutes on a Pi
  • Power pulled mid kernel upgrade = bricked screen, often inside a ceiling
  • We spent more time on recovery tooling than on the product
  • Lesson: the OS itself has to treat devices as cattle

2:00

  • Walk the stack bottom up: Pi, kernel + gadget snaps, read-only core24 base, snapd, app snaps
  • Then click through the four steps:
  • 1. Flash Ubuntu Core 24 with Raspberry Pi Imager and boot
  • 2. Everything is a signed snap: kernel, gadget, base and apps
  • 3. Updates are all or nothing; a failed one rolls back by itself
  • 4. Apps are confined and reach hardware only through interfaces
  • Takeaway: on Pi OS you configure a machine; on Ubuntu Core you declare a product and every device is a copy
  • If asked about models: inside the app snap or as their own snap, same signed updates and rollback
  • If asked why Snappy in 2016: it beat balena and Yocto on Screenly's checklist; boot time was the one weak spot

Choosing an edge OS: the honest comparison

Raspberry Pi OSYocto / BuildrootbalenaOSUbuntu Core
What it isGeneral-purpose DebianBuild-your-own LinuxContainer OS (Yocto-based)Immutable, snap-based Ubuntu
Appsapt packagesWhatever you build inDocker-compatible containersSnaps (Docker as a snap)
OS updatesIn place, no rollbackAdd Mender / RAUC / SWUpdateHost OS updates, rollbackTransactional, auto rollback
App isolationNone by defaultDIYContainersStrict confinement + interfaces
Fleet toolsDIY (Ansible, Puppet)DIY, Mender or hawkBitbalenaCloud / openBalenaSnap Store, Landscape
SupportFollows Debian releasesYou maintain it; LTS up to 4 yrsRolling; ESR lines 9 months10 yrs; 15 with Ubuntu Pro
Best forPrototypesCustom hardware, tiny imagesContainer-first teamsFleets that self-heal for years

Screenly shortlisted Snappy, balena and Yocto in 2016.

1:00

  • Keep it fair: every option has its place
  • Pi OS: great on the desk, but no rollback (the Puppet-era pain)
  • Yocto / Buildroot: smallest image, but you own the OS, the OTA and every patch
  • balenaOS: strong for container-first teams; A/B host OS updates with rollback too
  • Ubuntu Core: when devices must update themselves safely for a decade
  • Support row: Ubuntu Core 10 years standard, 15 with the Ubuntu Pro Legacy add-on

Field-ready hardware: what breaks first

💾 Storage fails first

Industrial-grade SD, 16 GB+, Class 10+. Endurance beats capacity.

⏳ Plan the lifespan

Even good cards last ~2 to 3 years under 24/7 writes.

🚀 Better storage

Pi 5 + NVMe HAT, or eMMC on a Compute Module.

🔌 Clean power

Official 27 W supply on Pi 5. Brownouts corrupt storage.

🌡️ Heat

Screens live in hot ceilings and kiosks. Use a heatsink or cooler.

🔐 Know the limits

No TPM on the Pi; RTC needs a battery. High security: x86 + TPM.

1:00

  • Cattle need the right hardware; storage fails first
  • Screenly ships SanDisk Industrial SD cards: players write 24/7, consumer cards can die in months
  • Even good cards last 2 to 3 years, so plan replacements; one site visit costs more than the card
  • Better: Pi 5 with an NVMe HAT, or eMMC on a Compute Module
  • Official 27 W supply on the Pi 5; brownouts corrupt storage
  • Ceilings and kiosks get hot: heatsink or active cooler
  • No TPM, RTC needs a battery: for high security, go x86 with a TPM
  • Card died anyway? Reflash, re-pair, content comes back because state lives in the cloud

Hardware access from a confined snap

  • Your app declares the hardware it needs: plugs and slots
  • Interfaces (camera, gpio, i2c, spi) replace root access
  • One command: snap connect impulse-runner:camera

📷 USB cameraeverything else: denied

On Pi OS your app is root. On Ubuntu Core it asks for exactly what it needs.

1:00

  • Cameras, sensors, GPIO: all through interfaces
  • impulse-runner (demo later) only sees the camera because I connected that interface
  • It can't touch anything else on the device
  • GPIO works the same way: snap connect my-app:gpio pi:bcm-gpio-17

Secure by design

Immutable. Confined. Signed.

  • Immutable: read-only root, signed snaps only
  • Confined: every app in its own sandbox
  • Signed model: defines what a device may run
  • Secure boot + FDE: on TPM/UEFI hardware
  • Pi 5 reality check: no TPM on the board, so no disk encryption
  • Need FDE? Screenly's x86 Max player has a TPM

1:30

  • Why it matters: a hacked kiosk is a way into the customer's network
  • Immutable: read-only root, only signed snaps run
  • Confined: every app in its own sandbox
  • Signed model assertion: defines what a device is allowed to run
  • Secure boot and full disk encryption: need TPM/UEFI hardware
  • Be upfront: the Pi 5 has no TPM, so no FDE
  • Customers who need FDE: Screenly's x86 Max player has a TPM

OTA updates that can't brick a device

  • Kernel, OS and apps update independently
  • Refresh windows and holds: you decide when
  • Validation sets pin a known-good set of snaps
  • Delta downloads keep updates small on slow links
1New revisionarrives from the store
→
2Installed alongsideold revision kept
→
3Restart + health checkhooks verify the app
→
✓ Healthy: commit
✗ Failed: roll back

1:30

  • Kernel, OS and apps update independently
  • Refresh windows and holds: you decide when updates land
  • Validation sets pin a known-good set of snaps
  • Deltas keep downloads small on slow links
  • The flow: new revision installs next to the old one, restart, health hooks run, then commit or roll back
  • At Screenly's scale it's been rock solid; only failures were dead SD cards and full disks
  • Compare the Puppet era: a pulled plug meant a bricked screen

One image + a claim code + state in the cloud = replace, don't repair

1:00

  • Same signed image on every player; nothing configured per device at the factory
  • First boot: joins the network, shows a pairing code
  • 8 lowercase characters, look-alikes (0, 1, i, l, o) removed, valid for 30 days
  • Installer types it in the dashboard; content, settings and updates follow
  • Dead card = reflash and re-pair

New valueprivate AI: data never leaves the device

1:00

  • So why am I talking about AI at all?
  • Screenly runs 10,000+ Ubuntu Core devices that show things
  • A physical AI device is the same box plus a camera and a model: it sees, decides, acts
  • Same problems: unattended, remote, always on
  • Same answers: signed updates, rollback, confinement, zero-touch provisioning
  • New value: private AI. Video stays on the device, only results leave
  • More and more companies can't or won't stream camera feeds to the cloud

Train with Edge Impulse

  • Model: collect, label and train in Edge Impulse, export one Linux .eim file tuned for the Pi
  • Device: impulse-runner, my open source confined snap; runs any Edge Impulse model on Core 22/24
  • New model = signed snap update, staged across the fleet, with rollback

Edge Impulse: the ML lifecycle in one place

🧩 Easy to start

Raw data to a trained model in your browser. No ML expertise needed.

📏 Hardware-aware

Shows latency, RAM and flash for your target before you deploy.

🔁 MLOps built in

One project for data, experiments and deploys. Scriptable via API + SDK.

📦 One file out

A Linux .eim holds DSP + model. It ships as a signed snap update.

1:00

  • This is the model side of the previous slide, as a loop
  • Collect: images from a phone or straight from the Pi camera
  • Label: AI-assisted labelling saves hours on object detection
  • Design the impulse: input, DSP and learning blocks
  • Train + tune: the EON Tuner tries block combinations for you
  • Test: model testing, then live classification on the Pi
  • Deploy: one Linux .eim file, shipped inside impulse-runner as a snap update
  • Then loop: new data from the field, retrain, ship again
  • Why I use it: easy to start, shows if a model fits the Pi before I deploy, and the API makes the MLOps loop scriptable

5 steps beyond the breadboard

  1. Package as a snap from week onesnapcraft init, with strict confinement on from the start
  2. Declare hardware with interfaces, never rootplugs: [camera, gpio] then snap connect
  3. Rehearse revert and recovery before you need themsnap revert my-app, and pull the plug mid-update on purpose
  4. Own your model assertion: the image is the productubuntu-image builds the same signed image in CI
  5. Use industrial SD cards; plan for 2 to 3 years of lifeOr NVMe / eMMC when the device writes all day
